{{Short description|Decision-making framework}}
The '''Five Safes''' is a framework for helping make decisions about making effective use of data which is confidential or sensitive. It is mainly used to describe or design research access to statistical data held by government and health agencies, and by data archives such as the [[UK Data Service]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is the Five Safes framework? |url=https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/secure-lab/what-is-the-five-safes-framework/ |access-date=2017-01-25 |website=www.ukdataservice.ac.uk |publisher=UK Data Service}}</ref> It is not an internationally accepted standard.

Two of the Five Safes refer to [[statistical disclosure control]], and so the Five Safes is usually used to contrast statistical and non-statistical controls when comparing [[data management]] options.

== Concept ==
The Five Safes proposes that data management decisions be considered as solving problems in five 'dimensions': projects, people, settings, data and outputs. The combination of the controls leads to 'safe use'. These are most commonly expressed as questions, for example:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Desai |first1=Tanvi |last2=Ritchie |first2=Felix |last3=Welpton |first3=Richard |year=2016 |title=Five Safes: designing data access for research |url=http://www2.uwe.ac.uk/faculties/BBS/Documents/1601.pdf |journal=Bristol Business School Working Papers in Economics |pages=Footnote 1}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/be4aa82cd8cf7f07ca2570d60018da27/e4d483bab4e1ad93ca257f4c00170bb6!OpenDocument |title=1015.0 - Information Paper: Transforming Statistics for the Future |date=2016 |website=www.abs.gov.au |publisher=Australian Bureau of Statistics |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref>
{| class="wikitable"
|Safe projects
|Is this use of the data appropriate?
|-
|Safe people
|Can the users be trusted to use it in an appropriate manner?
|-
|Safe settings
|Does the access facility limit unauthorised use?
|-
|Safe data
|Is there a disclosure risk in the data itself?
|-
|Safe outputs
|Are the statistical results non-disclosive?
|}
These dimensions are scales, not limits. That is, solutions can have a mix of more or fewer controls in each dimension, but the overall aim of 'safe use' independent of the particular mix. For example, a public use file available for open download cannot control who uses it, where or for what purpose, and so all the control (protection) must be in the data itself. In contrast, a file which is only accessed through a secure environment with certified users can contain very sensitive information: the non-statistical controls allow the data to be 'unsafe'. One academic likened the process to a graphic equalizer,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McEachern |first=Steve |year=2015 |title=Implementation of the Trusted Access Model |url=http://rsss.anu.edu.au/sites/default/files/SMcEachern_researcherperspective_ASSANov2015.pdf |journal=Australian Data Archive}}</ref> where bass and treble can be combined independently to produce a sound the listener likes, which has proven to be a very useful metaphor. This 2023 [[Dana Foundation|Data Foundation]] [https://datafoundation.org/news/past-events/217/217-The-Vision-of-Privacy-under-the-Evidence-Act-Exploring-the-Five-Safes webinar] is an expert discussion of how the elements interact, including an excellent introductory representation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hawes |first=Michael |title=The Five Safes Framework. Conference presentation: The Vision of Privacy under the Evidence Act |publisher=Data Foundation |year=2023}}</ref>

There is no 'order' to the Five Safes, in that one is necessarily more important than the others. However, Ritchie<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Felix |url=https://zenodo.org/record/897821 |title=The 'Five Safes': a framework for planning, designing and evaluating data access solutions |publisher=Data for Policy |year=2017 |doi=10.5281/zenodo.897821}}</ref> argued that the 'managerial' controls (projects, people, setting) should be addressed before the 'statistical' controls (data, output).

The Five Safes concept is associated with other topics which developed from the same programme at ONS, although these are not necessarily implemented. Safe people is associated with 'active researcher management',<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.unece.org/stats/documents/ece/ces/ge.46/2009/wp.15.e.pdf |title=Effective Researcher Management |last1=Desai |first1=Tanvi |last2=Ritchie |first2=Felix |date=2009 |website=www.unece.org |publisher=Eurostat |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> while safe outputs is linked with principles-based [[Statistical disclosure control|output statistical disclosure control]].

The Five Safes is a positive framework, describing what is and is not. The EDRU ('evidence-based, default-open, risk-managed, user-centred') attitudinal model<ref name=":7" /> is sometimes used to give a normative context

== The 'data access spectrum' ==
From 2003 the Five Safes was also represented in a simpler form as a 'Data Access Spectrum'.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ritchie |first=Felix |url=http://www.felixritchie.co.uk/publications/caed09v3.doc |title=Designing a national model for data access |date=2009 |work=Comparative Analysis of Enterprise (Micro)Data 2009 |access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> The non-data controls (project, people, setting, outputs) tend to work together, in that organisations often see these as a complementary set of restrictions on access. These can then be contrasted with choices about data anonymisation to present a linear representation of data access options. This presentation is consistent with the idea of 'data as a residual',<ref name=":6" /> as well as data protection laws of the time which often characterised data simply as anonymous or not anonymous.

A similar idea had already been developed independently in 2001 by Chuck Humphrey of the Canadian RDC network, the 'continuum of access'.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://slideplayer.com/slide/13350197/ |title=The Data Liberation Initiative Orientation Session |last=Humphrey |first=Charles (Chuck) |date=2001}}</ref> More recently, The [[Open Data Institute]] has developed a 'Data Spectrum toolkit'<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://theodi.org/about-the-odi/the-data-spectrum/ |title=ODI Data Spectrum |website=Open Data Institute |date=26 September 2020}}</ref> which includes industry-specific examples.

== History and terminology ==
The Five Safes was devised in the winter of 2002/2003 by Felix Ritchie at the UK [[Office for National Statistics]] (ONS) to describe its secure remote-access Virtual Microdata Laboratory (VML).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ritchie |first=Felix |year=2008 |title=Secure access to confidential microdata: four years of the Virtual Microdata Laboratory |url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/rel/elmr/economic-and-labour-market-review/no--5--may-2008/secure-access-to-confidential-microdata--four-years-of-the-virtual-microdata-laboratory.pdf |journal=Economic and Labour Market Statistics |volume=2 |issue=5 |pages=29–34 |doi=10.1057/elmr.2008.73 |s2cid=154673912}}</ref> It was described at this time as the 'VML Security Model'. This was adopted by the [[NORC at the University of Chicago|NORC]] data enclave,<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Lane |first1=Julia |author-link=Julia Lane |last2=Bowie |first2=Chet |last3=Scheuren |first3=Fritz |last4=Mulcahy |first4=Tim |year=2009 |title=NORC Data Enclave:Providing Secure Remote Access to Sensitive Microdata |url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1001617/4398365/S02P1-NORC-DATA-ENCLAVE-SCHEUREN.ppt |journal=UNECE/EU Workshop on Statistical Confidentiality 2009}}</ref> and more widely in the US, as the 'portfolio model' (although this is now also used to refer to a slightly different legal/statistical/educational breakdown).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lane |first1=Julia |last2=Heus |first2=Pascal |last3=Mulcahy |first3=Tim |s2cid=16923006 |year=2008 |title=Data Access in a Cyber World: Making Use of Cyberinfrastructure |journal=Transactions in Data Privacy |pages=2–16}}</ref> In 2012 the framework as was still being referred to as the 'VML security model',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Felix |first=Ritchie |date=2013-01-01 |title=International access to restricted data: A principles-based standards approach |journal=Statistical Journal of the IAOS |language=en |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=289–300 |doi=10.3233/sji-130780 |issn=1874-7655}}</ref> but its increasing use among non-UK organisations led to the adoption of the more general and informative phrase 'Five Safes'.<ref name=":0" />

The original framework only had four safes (projects, people, settings and outputs): the framework was used to describe highly detailed data access through a secure environment, and so the 'data' dimension was irrelevant. From 2007 onwards, 'safe data' was included as the framework was used to a describe a wider range of ONS activities. As the US version was based upon the 2005 specification, some US iterations uses have the original four dimensions (eg<ref name=":1" />).

Some discussions, such as the [[OECD]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.oecd.org/std/microdata-access-final-report-OECD-2014.pdf |title=OECD Expert Group For International Collaboration On Microdata Access, Chapter 6. Standardised Application Process For Microdata Access |last=Volkow |first=Natalia |website=www.oecd.org |publisher=OECD |pages=73–79 |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> use the term 'secure' instead 'safe'. However, the use of both these terms can cause presentational problems: less control in a particular dimension could be seen to imply 'unsafe users' or 'insecure settings', for example, which distracts from the main message. Hence, the Australian government uses the term "five [[data sharing]] principles".

The 'Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework'<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Elliot |first1=Mark |url=https://ukanon.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/The-Anonymisation-Decision-making-Framework.pdf |title=Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework |last2=Mackey |first2=Elaine |last3=O'Hara |first3=Kieran |last4=Tudor |first4=Caroline |publisher=University of Manchester |year=2016 |archive-date=2020-09-20 |access-date=2020-04-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920212553/https://ukanon.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/The-Anonymisation-Decision-making-Framework.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref> uses a framework based on the Five Safes but relabelling "projects", "people", and "settings" as "governance", "agency" and "infrastructure", respectively; "Output" is omitted, and "safe use" becomes "functional anonymisation". There is no reference to the Five Safes or any associated literature. The Australian version<ref>{{Cite book |last1=O'Keefe |first1=Christine |url=https://doi.org/10.4225/08/59c169433efd4 |title=De-identification decision-making framework |last2=Otorepec |first2=Stephanie |last3=Elliot |first3=Mark |last4=Mackay |first4=Elaine |last5=O'Hara |first5=Kieran |publisher=CSIRO |year=2017 |doi=10.4225/08/59c169433efd4}}</ref> was required to include references to the Five Safes, and presented it as an alternative without comment.

== Application ==
The framework has had three uses: pedagogical, descriptive, and design. Since 2016, it has also been used, directly and indirectly in legislation. See <ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Green |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Ritchie |first2=Felix |date=2023-11-30 |title=The present and future of the Five Safes framework |url=https://journalprivacyconfidentiality.org/index.php/jpc/article/view/831 |journal=Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality |language=en |volume=13 |issue=2 |doi=10.29012/jpc.831 |issn=2575-8527 |doi-access=free}}</ref> for more detailed examples.

=== Pedagogy ===
The first significant use of the framework, other than internal administrative use, was to structure researcher training courses at the UK Office for National Statistics from 2003. [[UK Data Archive]], [[Administrative Data Research Network]], [[Eurostat]], [[Statistics New Zealand]], the Mexican [[National Institute of Statistics and Geography (Mexico)|National Institute of Statistics and Geography]], [[NORC at the University of Chicago|NORC]], [[Statistics Canada]] and the [[Australian Bureau of Statistics]], amongst others, have also used this framework. Most of these courses are for researchers using restricted-access facilities; the Eurostat courses<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata/overview/self-study-material-for-microdata-users |title=Self-study material for the users of European microdatasets |website=ec.europa.eu |publisher=European Commission |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> are unusual in that they are designed for all users of sensitive data.

=== Description ===
The framework is often used to describe existing data access solutions (e.g. UK [[HM Revenue and Customs|HMRC]] Data Lab,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.slideserve.com/stephen-hester/the-hmrc-datalab |title=The HMRC Datalab |last=Hawkins |first=Mike |date=2011 |website=slideserve.com |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> UK Data Service,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=The 5 safes of access to confidential data |url=https://www.ukdataservice.ac.uk/news-and-events/eventsitem/?id=4058 |access-date=2017-01-25 |website=www.ukdataservice.ac.uk |publisher=UK Data Service |archive-date=2017-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202054324/https://www.ukdataservice.ac.uk/news-and-events/eventsitem/?id=4058 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Statistics New Zealand<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/stats/documents/ece/ces/ge.46/2013/Topic_3_NZ.pdf |title=Confidentiality for integrated data |last=Camden |first=Mike |date=2011 |website=www.unece.org |publisher=Eurostat |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref>) or planned/conceptualised ones (e.g. Eurostat in 2011<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/stats/documents/ece/ces/ge.46/2011/43_Eurostat.pdf |title=The Future of Access to European Confidential Data for Scientific Purposes |last1=Bujnowska |first1=Aleksandra |last2=Museux |first2=Jean-Marc |date=2011 |website=www.unece.org |publisher=Eurostat |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref>). An early use<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ritchie |first=Felix |year=2005 |title=Access to business microdata in the UK: dealing with the irreducible risks |url=http://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/stats/documents/ece/ces/ge.46/2005/wp.29.e.pdf |journal=UNECE/Eurostat Workshop on Statistical Data Confidentiality 2005}}</ref> was to help identify areas where ONS' still had 'irreducible risks' in its provision of secure remote access.

The framework is mostly used for confidential social science data. To date it appears to have made little impact on medical research planning,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Green |first=Elizabeth |year=2015 |others=et al |title=Enabling data linkage to maximise the value of public health research data |url=http://www.wellcome.ac.uk/stellent/groups/corporatesite/@policy_communications/documents/web_document/wtp059017.pdf |journal=Public Health Research Data Forum Commissioned Reports |publisher=Wellcome Trust}}</ref> although it is now included in the revised guidelines on implementing [[HIPAA]] regulations<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://www.nap.edu/catalog.php?record_id=18614 |title=Proposed Revisions to the Common Rule for the Protection of Human Subjects in the Behavioral and Social Sciences |last=Council |first=National Research |date=2014-01-09 |isbn=9780309298063 |language=en |doi=10.17226/18614 |pmid=25032406}}</ref> in the US, and by [[Cancer Research UK]] and the [[Health Foundation]] in the UK.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |url=https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/media/604145/19_5safes_safesettings_wolters.pdf |title=Governance and the HSCIC's IG toolkit |last=Wolters |first=Arne |date=2015 |website=ukdataservice.ac.uk |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> It has also been used to describe a security model for the Scottish [[Health informatics|Health Informatics]] Programme.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.rss.org.uk/uploadedfiles/userfiles/files/Frank-Sullivan-linkage.ppt |title=The Scottish Health Informatics Programme |last=Sullivan |first=Frank |website=www.rss.org.uk |access-date=2017-01-25}}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

=== Design ===
In general the Five Safes has been used to describe solutions post-factum, and to explain/justify choices made, but an increasing number of organisations have used the framework to design data access solutions. For example, the Hellenic Statistical Agency developed a data strategy built around the Five Safes in 2016; the UK Health Foundation used the Five Safes to design its data management and training programmes.<ref name=":4" /> Use in the private sector is less common but  some organisations have incorporated the Five Safes into consulting services.

In 2015 the UK Data Service organized a workshop<ref name=":3" /> to encourage data users from the academic and private sectors to think about how to manage confidential research data, using the Five Safes to demonstrate alternative options and [[best practice]].

Early adopters for strategic design use were in Australia: both the Australian Bureau of Statistics and the Australian Department of Social Service used the Five Safes as an ex ante design tool.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite news |url=http://eprints.uwe.ac.uk/31874/ |title=Department of Social Services data access project final report. Project Report |last1=Green |first1=Elizabeth |date=2016 |last2=Ritchie |first2=Felix}}</ref>  In 2017 the Australian [[Productivity Commission]] recommended<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.pc.gov.au/inquiries/completed/data-access/report |title=Data Availability and Use: Australian Productivity Commission Inquiry Report |publisher=Productivity Commission |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-74037-617-4}}</ref> adopting a version of the framework to support cross-government data sharing and re-use. This underwent extensive consultation and culminated in the DAT Act 2022. 

Since 2020 the Five Safes has been the overriding framework for the design of new secure facilities and data sharing arrangements in the UK for public health and social sciences. This has been promoted by the [[Office for Statistics Regulation]], the [[UK Statistics Authority]], [[NHS Digital|NHS DIgital]], and the research funding bodies [https://www.adruk.org/ Administrative Data Research UK] and [https://dareuk.org.uk/ DARE UK].

=== Regulation and legislation ===
Three laws have incorporated the Fives Safes. They are explicit in the South Australian [https://www.legislation.sa.gov.au/LZ/C/A/PUBLIC%20SECTOR%20(DATA%20SHARING)%20ACT%202016.aspx Public Sector (Data Sharing) Act 2016], and implicit in the research provisions of the UK [[Digital Economy Act 2017|Digital Economy Act]] 2017. The Australian [[Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022|Data Availability and Transparency Act]] 2022 renames the Five Safes as the Five Data Sharing Principles.A 2025 statutory review of the DAT Act 2022 found "that the DAT Act has not been effective in achieving its objectives."<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |url=https://www.finance.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-03/statutory-review-of-data-availability-and-transparency-act-final-report.pdf |title=Statutory Review of the Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022 – Final Report |last=Department of Finance |date=2025 |website=Commonwealth Department of Finance website |access-date=1 April 2026}}</ref>. The review includes specific references to the challenges associated with the Safes model being implemented in practice "The DAT Act’s current approach to the Five Safes is not strictly a principles-based approach, noting that they are embedded within and enabled through the DAT Act’s very prescriptive, rules-based approach."

== Public engagement ==
The UK Data Service has produced a blog<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://blog.ukdataservice.ac.uk/access-to-sensitive-data-for-research-the-5-safes/ |title=Access to sensitive data for research: the five safes |last1=Welpton |first1=Richard |last2=Corti |first2=Louise |website=blog.ukdataservice.ac.ukpublisher=UK Data Service |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> and video<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/embed/Mln9T52mwj0 |title=Five Safes video |website=www.youtube.com |publisher=UK Data Service |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> for the general public about the use of Five Safes in re-using administrative data. Statistics New Zealand produced a non-technical description,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.stats.govt.nz/browse_for_stats/snapshots-of-nz/integrated-data-infrastructure/keep-data-safe.aspx |title=How we keep IDI data safe |website=www.stats.govt.nzpublisher=Statistics New Zealand |access-date=2017-01-25}}</ref> as did ONS for [[Data Privacy Day]] 2017.
<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/ |title=The Five Safes: data privacy at ONS |last=Stokes |first=Pete |date=2017 |website=blog.ons.gov.uk |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=2017-01-28}}</ref>
The Australian Federal Government has produced several videos on data sharing, including the Data Sharing Principles.
<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.datacommissioner.gov.au/node/151 |title=Sharing data safely |last=Office of the National Data Commissioner |date=2022 |website=ONDC}}</ref>

== Criticism ==
In the 2020 paper, "Not fit for Purpose: A critical analysis of the ‘Five Safes’",
<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Culnane |first1=Chris |last2=Rubinstein |first2=Benjamin I. P. |last3=Watts |first3=David |title=Not fit for Purpose: A critical analysis of the 'Five Safes' |year=2020 |class=cs.CR |eprint=2011.02142}}</ref>
the authors argue that Five Safes is fundamentally flawed due to its disconnection from existing legal protections, its appropriation of safety notions without strong technical measures, and its static view of disclosure risk. Others have argued that the Five Safes has too little content to be useful, or is a box-ticking exercise, or that more 'safes' are needed. Green and Ritchie (2023)<ref name=":8" /> provide an extensive review of these critiques and proposals. International standards (such as ISO/IEC/JTC1) for data sharing and use should be considered for robust data sharing frameworks.
